Model-Agnostic Lifelong LLM Safety via Externalized Attack-Defense Co-Evolution

Xiaozhe Zhang1, Chaozhuo Li2, Hui Liu1, Shaocheng Yan3, Bingyu Yan4, Qiwei Ye5, Haoliang Li1
1City University of Hong Kong 2Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications 3Wuhan University
4Beihang University 5Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence
Abstract

Large language models remain vulnerable to adversarial prompts that elicit harmful outputs. Existing safety paradigms typically couple red-teaming and post-training in a closed, policy-centric loop, causing attack discovery to suffer from rapid saturation and limiting the exposure of novel failure modes, while leaving defenses inefficient, rigid, and difficult to transfer across victim models. To this end, we propose EvoSafety, an LLM safety framework built around persistent, inspectable, and reusable external structures. For red teaming, EvoSafety equips the attack policy with an adversarial skill library, enabling continued vulnerability probing through simple library expansion after saturation, while supporting the evolution of adversarial vectors. For defense learning, EvoSafety replaces model-specific safety fine-tuning with a lightweight auxiliary defense model augmented with memory retrieval. This enables efficient, transferable, and model-agnostic safety improvements, while allowing robustness to be enhanced solely through memory updates. With a single training procedure, the defense policy can operate in both Steer and Guard modes: the former activates the victim model’s intrinsic defense mechanisms, while the latter directly filters harmful inputs. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of EvoSafety: in Guard mode, it achieves a 99.61% defense success rate, outperforming Qwen3Guard-8B by 14.13% with only 37.5% of its parameters, while preserving reasoning performance on benign queries. Warning: This paper contains potentially harmful text.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) [51, 3, 71, 21, 4] have emerged as a foundational substrate of modern AI, catalyzing advances across diverse domains such as scientific discovery [9], software engineering [20], and beyond [11]. However, this broad capability is inherently dual-use: adversaries can exploit LLMs through jailbreaking or malicious prompting to elicit harmful outputs, posing serious safety risks [23, 44, 70]. Improving the safety of LLMs is therefore a prerequisite for their trustworthy and responsible deployment.

A common recipe for enhancing the safety of LLMs couples red-teaming with safety-oriented post-training [6, 28]. Red-teaming simulates an attacker that seeks to expose model vulnerabilities by constructing adversarial prompts that elicit harmful or policy-violating behaviors [55, 26]. To improve coverage and scalability, recent work has moved beyond manual prompt engineering [1, 19] toward automated pipelines [101, 90, 30], among which reinforcement learning (RL)-based methods have emerged as a leading paradigm, as they can adaptively discover and refine novel attack vectors [31, 81]. The successful attack samples collected through red-teaming are subsequently used to post-train LLMs from the defender’s perspective, where alignment techniques such as RLHF are applied to steer model behavior toward greater safety [6, 37].

Despite this progress, learning for both attack and defense remains largely monolithic, with offensive and defensive knowledge internalized within the parameters of the policy, as illustrated in Fig. 1(a). Consequently, safety improvement becomes tightly coupled to a specific victim model and training snapshot [6, 37], forcing re-optimization whenever the victim changes. Such limitations are particularly severe for large-scale frontier models, for which fine-tuning is substantially more resource-intensive. On the offensive side, policies optimized against a surrogate victim model often exploit model-specific vulnerabilities, producing highly tailored adversarial prompts that are effective against the surrogate but fail to generalize to unseen victim models [42]. Moreover, once optimization terminates, their offensive capability tends to plateau, reflecting a limited capacity to continually discover and evolve novel attack vectors [53], which in turn constrains sustained safety improvement. These limitations raise a central question:

Inspired by the view that human civilization progresses through the continual externalization of cognitive burdens [12, 68], we argue that granting both sides of the safety game access to external knowledge is crucial for advancing LLM safety. From the offensive perspective, if attack-relevant knowledge is externalized and made accessible to the attack policy during training, such a design offers two key benefits. First, a more capable attacker can uncover long-tail vulnerabilities that would otherwise remain hidden. Second, the policy can continue to incorporate distilled knowledge after training, enabling sustained exploration beyond the saturation point, even in a zero-shot setting. Each of these can drive stronger safety improvements [99]. From the defensive side, if safety knowledge is no longer parameter-bound but is instead instantiated as prompt-level defense mechanisms, defensive capabilities can transfer across model updates without repeated safety retraining and remain extensible to emerging adversarial prompts.

To this end, we introduce EvoSafety, a framework that augments both sides of the safety game with persistent, inspectable, and reusable external structures, as illustrated in Fig. 1(b). On the offensive side, EvoSafety moves beyond end-to-end adversarial prompt generation by reformulating the attack policy as a skill execution engine, which composes and executes explicit skills from an Adversarial Skill Library. Each skill is distilled from heterogeneous attack knowledge into a structured, validated, and inducible representation. On the defensive side, EvoSafety shifts optimization from the victim model itself to a lightweight Auxiliary Defense Model. Conditioned on historically successful attacks stored in a Verified Memory Bank, this model synthesizes input-adaptive, model-agnostic safety prefixes in two complementary modes: Steer, which activates intrinsic safeguards within victim models, and Guard, which filters harmful inputs before inference. Both modes eliminate the need for model-specific safety fine-tuning. Moreover, prefix generation can be further improved through simple memory expansion, requiring no additional training while providing more informative references for defense synthesis.

We optimize both the attack and defense policies through RL. For the attacker, RL bridges the gap between the utilization of external skills and the evolution of novel attack vectors. For the defender, RL enables a favorable balance between safety and over-defensiveness [5]. Furthermore, to account for the non-stationarity inherent in adversarial interactions [74] and to better approximate a dynamic threat environment during training, we iteratively update both policies within a co-evolutionary training loop. Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We introduce EvoSafety, a framework that equips both attack and defense policies with external structures. By mitigating attack saturation and eliminating model-specific safety fine-tuning, EvoSafety supports lifelong, model-agnostic safety improvement.

  • •

    EvoSafety is a co-evolutionary framework that demonstrates steady performance gains across rounds. To our knowledge, EvoSafety is the first RL-driven approach that bridges external skill use and the evolving landscape of novel attack vectors.

  • •

    Experiments demonstrate that EvoSafety significantly strengthens safety without compromising general reasoning ability. In Guard mode, it achieves a 98.83% defense success rate against unseen attacks and outperforms Qwen3Guard while using fewer parameters.

2 Related Work

Red-Teaming. Early red-teaming relied on manual prompt engineering and crowdsourced evaluations to identify systematic vulnerabilities in deployed LLMs [55, 45, 79]. While effective, these approaches are labor-intensive, difficult to scale, and insufficient for covering broad failure modes [6, 26]. This has motivated automated red-teaming: early methods searched the input space [103, 13], whereas recent agentic frameworks autonomously conduct evaluations and incorporate external attack strategies [87, 97, 101, 57]. However, without fine-grained feedback, they can suffer from low attack success rates and poor efficiency [90]. Recent RL-based red-teaming [86, 81, 75, 15] instead optimizes attack policies directly for jailbreak rewards, leveraging advances in RL for LLM reasoning [66, 64]. Yet these methods are prone to mode collapse and homogeneous attacks [31], and often saturate in static, closed environments, limiting the discovery of novel jailbreak vectors.

Safety Alignment and Improvement Existing LLM safety mechanisms mainly follow two paradigms: internalized alignment during training and externalized control at inference. Training-time defenses encode safety behavior into model parameters through pretraining or fine-tuning alignment [37, 93, 8]. Although principled, they often remain fragile under attacks and may induce over-refusal or utility degradation [29]; they also require repeated training for different target models [102]. In contrast, inference-time defenses are more modular and easier to iterate without modifying the base model, ranging from safety-oriented prompting [56, 95], to prompted self-scrutiny [83], to safety demonstrations [78].

Multi-Agent Adversarial Co-evolution Recent LLM safety research has increasingly adopted iterative co-evolution, where both sides of the safety game are jointly refined. SSP [73] uses a self-evolving framework [35], with a single LLM acting as both attacker and defender during training. MAGIC [80] decouples these roles and enhances the attacker with chain-of-thought reasoning [77]. TriPlay-RL [69] further introduces a judge model into the RL loop for finer-grained safety evaluation. Despite improving safety, these methods keep safety-related knowledge parameter-bound, leading to saturation and limited transferability.

3 Methodology

3.1 Overview

Fig. 2 illustrates the architecture of EvoSafety, a co-evolutionary framework designed to iteratively optimize an Attack Policy πA\pi_{A} (Section 3.2) and a Defense Policy πD\pi_{D} (Section 3.3). For a given request rr, the process begins with the Skill Retriever fetching two expert skills ese_{s} from the Adversarial Skill Library to condition πA\pi_{A}, which in turn generates an adversarial prompt ata_{t}. Subsequently, the Memory Retriever identifies the top-2 relevant successful historical attacks eme_{m} from the Verified Memory Bank. These retrieved memories serve as references for πD\pi_{D} to produce a safety prefix dtd_{t} tailored to ata_{t}. The frozen victim model 𝒯\mathcal{T} then processes the concatenated input [dt;at][d_{t};a_{t}] to yield response yty_{t}, from which rewards are derived to update both policies. This process is detailed in Algorithm 1, where πA\pi_{A} and πD\pi_{D} are iteratively optimized in the co-evolutionary loop:

𝒥i​(πA,πD)\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{i}(\pi_{A},\pi_{D}) ≔𝔼at∼πA(⋅∣r,es),dt∼πD(⋅∣em,at),yt∼𝒯(⋅∣at,dt)[ℛi(r,at,dt,yt)],\displaystyle\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{\,a_{t}\sim\pi_{A}(\cdot\mid r,e_{s}),\,d_{t}\sim\pi_{D}(\cdot\mid e_{m},a_{t}),\,y_{t}\sim\mathcal{T}(\cdot\mid a_{t},d_{t})}\!\left[\mathcal{R}_{i}(r,a_{t},d_{t},y_{t})\right], (1)
πi\displaystyle\pi_{i} ←argmaxπi𝒥i(πA,πD),i∈{A,D},\displaystyle\leftarrow\arg\max_{\pi_{i}}\mathcal{J}_{i}(\pi_{A},\pi_{D}),\qquad i\in\{A,D\},

where ℛi\mathcal{R}_{i} denotes the corresponding reward function for i∈{A,D}i\in\{A,D\}.

After training, the learned defense policy πD\pi_{D} can be deployed in two distinct modes: Steer and Guard. Given a new prompt atnewa_{t}^{\mathrm{new}} (potentially harmful or benign) and an arbitrary new victim model 𝒯new\mathcal{T}^{\mathrm{new}}, both modes first sample a defense prefix dt∼πD(⋅∣em,atnew)d_{t}\sim\pi_{D}(\cdot\mid e_{m},a_{t}^{\mathrm{new}}). In Steer mode, the final response yty_{t} is generated by prepending the prefix to the prompt: yt∼𝒯new​([dt;atnew])y_{t}\sim\mathcal{T}^{\mathrm{new}}\!\left([d_{t}\,;\,a_{t}^{\mathrm{new}}]\right). This mode aims to steer the victim model’s internal latent states to activate its intrinsic safety mechanisms, thereby eliciting a harmless response. In Guard mode, the system treats dtd_{t} as a diagnostic signal. If dtd_{t} is predicted to trigger a refusal from the victim model, the input is filtered; otherwise, the system proceeds with a standard rollout. Further details are provided in Appendix A.3.2.

3.2 Attack Policy Learning with Skills

For each request rr, the Skill Retriever extracts a subset of skills from the Adversarial Skill Library 𝒮\mathcal{S}, denoted as 𝒮⁡(r)={s1,…,sk}⊆𝒮\mathcal{S}(r)=\{s_{1},\dots,s_{k}\}\subseteq\mathcal{S}. Each skill s∈𝒮⁡(r)s\in\mathcal{S}(r) comprises an executable transformation script ses_{e} and its corresponding attack schema sss_{s}. Applying ses_{e} to the request rr yields a transformed artifact su=se​(r)s_{u}=s_{e}(r), along with a binary indicator sz∈{Success,Failure}s_{z}\in\{\texttt{Success},\texttt{Failure}\} that denotes whether the attack successfully compromised a surrogate victim model. These signals are subsequently aggregated into a structured context crc_{r}, which guides the attack policy πA\pi_{A} in generating the final adversarial prompt ata_{t}:

cr=(r,{(su,sz,ss)}s∈𝒮⁡(r)),at∼πA(⋅∣cr).c_{r}=\left(r,\{(s_{u},s_{z},s_{s})\}_{s\in\mathcal{S}(r)}\right),\qquad a_{t}\sim\pi_{A}(\cdot\mid c_{r}). (2)

3.2.1 Adversarial Skill Library

Heterogeneous Attack Artifacts and Structured Skill Representation. Expert-crafted attack strategies manifest in heterogeneous forms, ranging from executable code to natural language descriptions. To cover a broader spectrum of attack vectors, we incorporate all such artifacts and leverage the proposed Dual-Path Skill Grounding to map them into a unified structured representation.

Each skill is encapsulated by an executable script and a corresponding Markdown specification. The script converts standard requests into adversarial rewrites and may incorporate external APIs or local models to assist generation or enable gray-box attacks. The Markdown file documents the skill’s identity, provenance, and a high-level attack schema abstracted from the script. This dual representation preserves both execution details and strategic logic, thereby facilitating downstream skill induction and improving the generalization of attack policies.

Tri-Axis Skill Validation. We implement multi-stage filtering to retain only skills that meet three criteria. (1) Functional validity measures the effectiveness of a skill via its attack success rate. (2) Schema consistency evaluates the fidelity of the derived high-level attack schema. (3) Behavioral diversity encourages each candidate skill to differ from the existing skill set.

Skill Family Induction. We use the executable scripts and attack schemas of the validated skills to synthesize additional skills that follow the same strategic schema while differing in execution. The synthesized skills are then filtered using Tri-Axis Skill Validation, yielding a scalable adversarial skill library. Further details are provided in Appendix A.2.3.

3.2.2 Reward Design

A standard paradigm in RL-based training relies on a safety evaluator to score the surrogate victim model’s response yty_{t}. For a multi-tiered evaluator (e.g., Qwen3Guard 96), we convert the evaluation result into a discrete scalar reward:

ℛjudge​(r,yt)∈{0​(Safe),12​(Controversial), 1​(Unsafe)}.\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{judge}}(r,y_{t})\in\left\{0\penalty\ \text{(Safe)},\penalty\ \frac{1}{2}\penalty\ \text{(Controversial)},\penalty\ 1\penalty\ \text{(Unsafe)}\right\}. (3)

However, as shown in Appendix A.2.1, optimizing the attacker solely to maximize ℛjudge\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{judge}} can induce reward hacking 25: responses elicited by the generated prompts may receive high rewards while deviating from the intent specified by rr. Existing methods 24, 85 address this issue with a post-hoc semantic-similarity gate between yty_{t} and rr, discarding samples whose similarity falls below a predefined threshold. However, such late-stage filtering still requires querying the victim model 𝒯\mathcal{T} with out-of-distribution prompts, incurring unnecessary computational overhead.

To this end, we introduce Early-Stage Alignment Gating, which uses intent retention in the trajectory space as a robust proxy for final response alignment, yielding the following gated objective:

ℛA(r,at,dt,yt)=𝕀[sim(at,r)>τ]⋅ℛjudge(r,yt),\mathcal{R}_{A}(r,a_{t},d_{t},y_{t})=\mathbb{I}[\mathrm{sim}(a_{t},r)>\tau]\cdot\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{judge}}(r,y_{t}), (4)

where 𝕀⁡[⋅]\mathbb{I}[\cdot] denotes the indicator function, sim⁡(⋅,⋅)\mathrm{sim}(\cdot,\cdot) is a similarity metric, and τ\tau is the threshold. We prove its theoretical validity in Appendix A.2.2.

3.3 Defense Policy Learning with Memory

To provide empirical references for safety-prefix generation and reduce the optimization burden, we avoid requiring the Auxiliary Defense Model πD\pi_{D} to learn a complex prompt-to-prefix mapping entirely from scratch. Instead, we equip it with a lightweight yet effective Verified Memory Bank ℬ={a(i)}i=1N\mathcal{B}=\{a^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N}, which stores only historical adversarial prompts. Given a new prompt ata_{t}, πD\pi_{D} first retrieves a support set 𝒩k​(at)⊂ℬ\mathcal{N}_{k}(a_{t})\subset\mathcal{B} containing the top-kk semantically similar past attacks via efficient vector-based retrieval, and then generates the defense prefix according to

dt∼πD(⋅∣at,𝒩k(at)).d_{t}\sim\pi_{D}\!\left(\cdot\mid a_{t},\mathcal{N}_{k}(a_{t})\right). (5)

Owing to the simplicity of this memory bank design, our method can be efficiently expanded as new adversarial prompts are observed.

3.3.1 Reward Design

A straightforward approach is to train the defense policy using the negative of ℛjudge​(r,yt)\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{judge}}(r,y_{t}) in Eq. 3 as the reward. However, as discussed in Appendix A.3.1, optimizing this objective solely on harmful requests can lead to degenerate solutions: the policy may learn input-agnostic refusal patterns, such as producing a generic refusal prefix. To avoid this reward hacking, we instead define the reward over a mixture of benign and adversarial requests.

For benign requests r∈𝒟benr\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ben}}, responses are scored by a correctness indicator 𝕀corr​(yt)∈{0,1}\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{corr}}(y_{t})\in\{0,1\}. We construct 𝒟ben\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ben}} offline from queries on which a surrogate model is consistently correct with low output variance, so that low rewards are more likely to reflect safety-prefix-induced errors rather than intrinsic reasoning uncertainty. While this filtering improves attribution, it also eliminates most intra-group ranking signals under GRPO 66: completions often receive identical rewards, yielding near-zero or unstable advantages 100. We therefore augment the benign-request reward with a length-shaping term, which provides a denser learning signal while penalizing unnecessary verbosity:

ℛD​(r,at,dt,yt)={𝕀corr​(yt)​[α+β​(1−|yt|Lmax)+],r∈𝒟ben,v,v∈{0​(Unsafe),12​(Controversial), 1​(Safe)},r∈𝒟adv,\mathcal{R}_{D}(r,a_{t},d_{t},y_{t})=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{corr}}(y_{t})\left[\alpha+\beta\left(1-\frac{|y_{t}|}{L_{\max}}\right)^{+}\right],&r\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ben}},\\[11.99998pt] \displaystyle v,\quad v\in\left\{0\ \mathrm{(Unsafe)},\ \frac{1}{2}\ \mathrm{(Controversial)},\ 1\ \mathrm{(Safe)}\right\},&r\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{adv}},\end{cases} (6)

where (x)+=max⁡(x,0)(x)^{+}=\max(x,0) and LmaxL_{\max} denotes the maximum allowed response length. For benign requests, incorrect responses are assigned zero reward, whereas correct responses are further distinguished using a length-normalized shaping term. We set the base correctness reward to α=0.8\alpha=0.8 and the shaping coefficient to β=0.2\beta=0.2. For adversarial requests (r∈𝒟advr\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{adv}}), the reward is obtained by directly mapping the judge model’s safety classification to a scalar value.

4 Experiments and Results

4.1 Experimental Setup

Models. We initialize the attack policy from Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3. To improve defensive efficiency, we use Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct as the auxiliary defense model. For retrieval, we adopt Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B [94] as the embedding backbone. We further employ Qwen3Guard-Gen-8B [96] for two purposes: providing reward signals during training and serving as the safety/refusal judge during evaluation.

Adversarial Skill Library and Verified Memory Bank. We partition the Attack Skill Library into an initial attack skill library, used for training, and a held-out attack skill library, used to evaluate out-of-library generalization and the framework’s capacity for sustained evolution. We also maintain a Verified Memory Bank as a growing repository of concrete adversarial prompts. We initialize this bank with adversarial prompts from WildJailbreak [38] and continually expand it with prompts generated by attacker rollouts during training.

Datasets and Metrics. We construct adversarial training data from AdvBench [16], CategoricalQA [7], HarmfulQA [8], DangerousQA [65], and PKU-SafeRLHF [37], following prior work [31, 73]. The constraint-satisfying benign examples used for RL-based defense training are sampled from GSM8K [17]. For evaluation, we adopt the standard HarmBench [48] behaviors to assess both attack and defense methods, and report attack success rate (ASR) to measure offensive effectiveness and defensive robustness. To examine whether improved defensive behavior trades off with general capabilities, we further evaluate on GSM8K [17] and MMLU [33].

Implementation Details. Both the attack and defense policies are first trained with supervised fine-tuning (SFT). We use the same configuration for both policies: LoRA with rank 32, a learning rate of 1×10−51\times 10^{-5}, 1 epoch, a batch size of 128, and gradient accumulation over 4 steps. For RL training, both policies use LoRA with rank 64, a batch size of 32, and 16 rollouts per sample. The attacker is trained with a learning rate of 3×10−63\times 10^{-6} for [200,200,100,100][200,200,100,100] steps across rounds, while the auxiliary defense model is trained with a learning rate of 1×10−61\times 10^{-6} for [250,250,100,100][250,250,100,100] steps. All training is implemented with VERL [67] on 16 NVIDIA H100 GPUs.

Further details are provided in Appendix B.

4.2 RQ1 [Adversariality]: How Capable Is EvoSafety at Generating Attacks?

[RQ1-1] Main Attack Performance. We evaluate the attacker under both Qwen3Guard [96] and GPT-4.1 as LLM-as-a-Judge to rule out the possibility that high ASR is driven by evaluator overfitting during training. As shown in Tab. 1, our method significantly outperforms the RL-based baseline Jailbreak-R1 [31] by 65.3% in ASR, and even surpasses the state-of-the-art multi-turn method ICON [43] by 2.6% with a single interaction. In Appendix D.1, we demonstrate the capability of our framework to evolve novel attack vectors autonomously.

[RQ1-2] Zero-shot Attack Performance on New Skills. We further retrieve skills from the held-out attack skill library to assess generalization. As shown in the last row of Tab. 1, the performance drops marginally and remains superior to most multi-turn methods, with a 12.18% higher average ASR. This indicates that the attacker learns how to exploit diverse skills effectively, enabling the continual discovery of novel attack vectors simply by expanding the skill library with newly extracted skills, without requiring attacker retraining.

[RQ1-3] Scalability. We also evaluate the attacker’s ability to convert extra attempt budgets into higher ASR. We define ASR@NN as the fraction of harmful queries for which at least one jailbreak succeeds within NN attempts. As shown in Fig. 3, small open-weight models reach 100% success with just N=2N=2, while GPT-5.1 requires only five attempts.

4.3 RQ2 [Robustness]: How Effective Is EvoSafety at Improving Safety?

[RQ2-1] Can Our Defender Activate the Victim Model’s Intrinsic Safety? We evaluate defense performance against skill-unseen method (entirely OOD), i.e., Jailbreak-R1 [31]; skill-seen methods, i.e., CodeAttack [61] and GPTFuzz [89]; and the co-evolved matched attacker.11 1 The distinction between skill-seen methods and skill-unseen methods lies in whether the skills distilled from these methods were used during the training process of our co-evolution framework. The test set comprises all HarmBench [48] samples that successfully attack the victim model. As shown in Tab. 2, our method delivers the strongest defensive performance across almost all attack types and model scales. It reduces the average ASR from 19.92% under TriPlay-RL [69], the strongest baseline and a co-evolutionary method, to 11.62%, corresponding to a relative reduction of over 40%. Meanwhile, it better preserves general reasoning ability (-0.29 vs. -2.15).

[RQ2-2] Can Our Defender Serve as a Zero-Shot LLM Guard? We investigate whether an Auxiliary Defense Model, trained only once, can be repurposed as a zero-shot LLM guard. Mainstream baselines such as Llama-Guard [47] and Qwen3Guard [96] are evaluated under the Moderating User Prompt setting, rather than the Moderating Model Response setting. As shown in Tab. 3, our 3B model achieves a nearly 100% filtering success rate on attack-successful prompts, while using substantially fewer parameters and outperforming Llama-Guard and Qwen3Guard by 24.92% and 14.13%, respectively. Moreover, our method yields negligible false positives on benign inputs.

[RQ2-3] Can Memory Expansion Enhance Safety Without Additional Training? Finally, we examine whether defense performance can be further improved by directly adding current adversarial prompts to the Verified Memory Bank, without any additional parameter updates. We denote this memory-expanded variant as Ours+. As shown in Tab. 2 and Tab. 3, this lightweight extension consistently improves performance across both modes. Notably, in Guard mode, our method achieves a 100% success rate against entirely unseen attack vectors on both 4B and 70B victim models.

4.4 RQ3 [Co-evolution]: Do Attack and Defense Policies Evolve in Iterative Training?

Across training rounds, all learned attack and defense policies are evaluated against fixed counterparts to ensure protocol consistency. To broaden evaluation coverage beyond retriever-selected skills, we remove the skill retriever and test on randomly sampled skill combinations. As shown in Fig. 4, both models improve steadily across rounds, suggesting effective adversarial co-evolution.

4.5 RQ4 [Continual Evolution]: Can EvoSafety Support Lifelong Safety Improvement?

As demonstrated in Tab. 2 and Tab. 3, while our model achieves competitive zero-shot defense against OOD attacks, we further investigate whether incorporating distilled skills from these novel threats can elevate the robustness ceiling. To this end, we treat attack methods from the held-out attack library as nascent OOD signals and conduct incremental training on the extracted skills to evaluate their potential defense gains. As shown in Table 4,in Steer mode, the ASR on Llama-3.1-70B is reduced by over 5×\times relative to the baseline, from 12.54% to 2.31%. Meanwhile, in Guard mode with memory update, our method achieves 100% defense success across both 4B and 8B models, with no performance degradation on previously defended attack methods or general reasoning benchmarks. These results demonstrate that our approach can continuously adapt to newly emerging attack strategies, facilitating a step toward lifelong defense.

4.6 RQ5 [Ablation Study]: Are EvoSafety’s Components Effective?

[RQ5-1: Defense Policy]. We ablate a key component, memory retrieval, and observe its impact on activating intrinsic safety in Steer mode. Specifically, we restrict the model to generate the safety prefix solely from the current user prompt. As shown in Tab. 5, disabling memory increases the average ASR of adversarial prompts by approximately 2×\times, demonstrating the advantage of leveraging historical experience rather than generating prefixes from scratch.

[RQ5-2: Attack Policy]. We ablate three key factors: skill integration, the number of invoked skills, and the inclusion of the high-level attack schema. As shown in Tab. 5, removing skill integration confines optimization to a closed environment and substantially degrades performance, resulting in an average drop of 36.5% and a maximum drop of 51.5%. Interestingly, increasing the number of skills does not yield monotonic gains; using four skills instead produces the weakest performance on both the 4B and 70B models. Finally, removing the attack schema leads to a small but consistent reduction in effectiveness.

5 Conclusion

In summary, we introduce EvoSafety, a co-evolutionary framework that augments both attack and defense policies with external structures. EvoSafety redefines the attack policy as a skill execution engine and leverages RL to bridge skill exploitation and the discovery of novel attack vectors, effectively mitigating the diversity saturation issue in prior work. On the defense side, EvoSafety enables model-agnostic safety improvement, eliminating the need for repeated retraining for each victim model and enabling further safety improvements through memory updates alone. Furthermore, EvoSafety supports lifelong evolution by enabling continuous vulnerability probing with newly discovered skills, thereby driving iterative improvements in defensive capabilities. Extensive experiments show that EvoSafety outperforms mainstream baselines such as Qwen3Guard while using fewer parameters, while preserving benign reasoning performance.

Appendix Contents

Appendix A Methodology

A.1 Overreview

The details of the co-evolutionary iterative training process of EvoSafety are shown in Algorithm 1. In each round, we first train the attack policy and then train the defense policy.

A.2 Attack Policy

A.2.1 Analysis of Reward Hacking

As shown in Fig. 5, using attack success rate alone as the reward signal for the attack policy leads to severe reward hacking. Specifically, as training progresses, the sample-level training reward continues to increase, while the generated adversarial prompts gradually fail to preserve the intent of the given harmful request. Fig. 5(b) illustrates one such case: although the original request aims to obtain a social security number, the generated adversarial prompt contains only response-formatting rules. We attribute this behavior to overfitting to the safety evaluator. That is, even when the adversarial prompt does not reliably induce harmful responses from the victim model, the evaluator still assigns it a high reward, causing the attack policy to exploit evaluator-specific artifacts rather than optimize for genuinely intent-preserving adversarial behavior.

A.2.2 Theoretical Motivation: Prompt-Side Similarity as an Efficient Gating Signal

Let xx denote the original harmful request, pp the adversarial prompt generated by the attacker, and yy the response produced by the victim model 𝒯\mathcal{T}. Existing methods often enforce intent preservation by thresholding the response-side similarity sim⁡(x,y)\mathrm{sim}(x,y). While this criterion is conceptually direct, it is only observable after querying 𝒯\mathcal{T}, making it costly to integrate into training. To reduce this dependency, we consider gating on the prompt-side similarity sim⁡(x,p)\mathrm{sim}(x,p), which is available prior to victim-model inference and therefore incurs no additional query overhead.

Our goal in this section is not to prove that prompt-side similarity is universally interchangeable with response-side similarity. Instead, we provide a local theoretical motivation for treating sim⁡(x,p)\mathrm{sim}(x,p) as a computationally efficient candidate signal for intent-preserving gating, and we later assess its practical usefulness empirically.

Setup.

Let ϕ⁡(⋅)∈ℝd\phi(\cdot)\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denote a sentence embedding function (e.g., Sentence-BERT 60). We assume L2-normalized embeddings:

‖ϕ⁡(z)‖2=1,∀z.\|\phi(z)\|_{2}=1,\qquad\forall z. (7)

Thus cosine similarity reduces to inner product:

sp=⟨ϕ⁡(x),ϕ⁡(p)⟩,sy=⟨ϕ⁡(x),ϕ⁡(y)⟩.s_{p}=\langle\phi(x),\phi(p)\rangle,\qquad s_{y}=\langle\phi(x),\phi(y)\rangle. (8)

The response is generated autoregressively:

y∼P𝒯(⋅∣p),P𝒯(yt∣p,y<t)=softmax(Woht(p,y<t)),y\sim P_{\mathcal{T}}(\cdot\mid p),\qquad P_{\mathcal{T}}(y_{t}\mid p,y_{<t})=\mathrm{softmax}\!\big(W_{o}h_{t}(p,y_{<t})\big), (9)

where hth_{t} is the hidden state. We analyze the conditional expectation of the response-side similarity:

𝔼[sy∣p]=𝔼y∼P𝒯(⋅∣p)[⟨ϕ(x),ϕ(y)⟩].\mathbb{E}[s_{y}\mid p]=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim P_{\mathcal{T}}(\cdot\mid p)}\big[\langle\phi(x),\phi(y)\rangle\big]. (10)

Define the conditional mean response representation:

g(p):=𝔼y∼P𝒯(⋅∣p)[ϕ(y)].g(p):=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim P_{\mathcal{T}}(\cdot\mid p)}[\phi(y)]. (11)

By linearity of expectation,

𝔼⁡[sy∣p]=⟨ϕ⁡(x),g⁡(p)⟩.\mathbb{E}[s_{y}\mid p]=\langle\phi(x),g(p)\rangle. (12)
Local semantic correspondence.

In autoregressive language models, each token is generated conditioned on the prefix (p,y<t)(p,y_{<t}) 72. Consequently, the prompt can influence the distribution of generated responses through the decoding trajectory. Prior work has also shown that variations in prompts can induce systematic changes in model outputs 58, 10, 52. We use this observation only as motivation for a local approximation of the conditional mean response representation.

Proof.

Substituting the local first-order approximation g⁡(p)=W​ϕ​(p)+b+ε⁡(p)g(p)=W\phi(p)+b+\varepsilon(p) into 𝔼⁡[sy∣p]=⟨ϕ⁡(x),g⁡(p)⟩\mathbb{E}[s_{y}\mid p]=\langle\phi(x),g(p)\rangle, we obtain

𝔼⁡[sy∣p]=⟨ϕ⁡(x),W​ϕ​(p)⟩+⟨ϕ⁡(x),b⟩+⟨ϕ⁡(x),ε⁡(p)⟩.\mathbb{E}[s_{y}\mid p]=\langle\phi(x),W\phi(p)\rangle+\langle\phi(x),b\rangle+\langle\phi(x),\varepsilon(p)\rangle. (16)

Using the identity ⟨a,W​b⟩=⟨W⊤​a,b⟩\langle a,Wb\rangle=\langle W^{\top}a,b\rangle, this becomes

𝔼⁡[sy∣p]=⟨W⊤​ϕ​(x),ϕ⁡(p)⟩+c+r⁡(p),\mathbb{E}[s_{y}\mid p]=\langle W^{\top}\phi(x),\phi(p)\rangle+c+r(p), (17)

where c=⟨ϕ⁡(x),b⟩c=\langle\phi(x),b\rangle and r⁡(p)=⟨ϕ⁡(x),ε⁡(p)⟩r(p)=\langle\phi(x),\varepsilon(p)\rangle. Finally, by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and the unit-norm assumption ‖ϕ⁡(x)‖=1\|\phi(x)\|=1, we have

|r⁡(p)|=|⟨ϕ⁡(x),ε⁡(p)⟩|≤‖ϕ⁡(x)‖|ε⁡(p)|≤δ.|r(p)|=|\langle\phi(x),\varepsilon(p)\rangle|\leq\|\phi(x)\|\,\|\varepsilon(p)\|\leq\delta. (18)

This completes the proof. ∎

Implications for Early-Stage Alignment Gating Mechanism.

The proposition shows that, under a local linearization assumption, the expected response-side similarity is a linear score over the prompt embedding ϕ⁡(p)\phi(p). Prompt-side similarity,

sp=⟨ϕ⁡(x),ϕ⁡(p)⟩,s_{p}=\langle\phi(x),\phi(p)\rangle, (19)

is also a linear score over the same representation. This provides a theoretical motivation for using sps_{p} as a computationally efficient signal for early-stage intent-preserving gating.

Importantly, this argument does not establish that sps_{p} is a universally reliable or monotonic substitute for response-side similarity. In general, 𝔼⁡[sy∣p]\mathbb{E}[s_{y}\mid p] depends on the direction W⊤​ϕ​(x)W^{\top}\phi(x), whereas sps_{p} depends on the direction ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x). These two directions need not coincide. Therefore, the strength of prompt-side similarity as a proxy depends on the empirical alignment between these directions, the size of the local approximation error, and the variability of sampled responses around their conditional mean.

Accordingly, we treat prompt-side similarity as a motivated and computationally cheap candidate proxy, rather than as a guaranteed surrogate. Its practical reliability is evaluated empirically in Figure 6. When the empirical correlation is sufficiently strong, replacing response-side similarity with prompt-side similarity can reduce victim-model queries during training while preserving an effective early-stage filtering signal.

A.2.3 Adversarial Skill Library

Dual-Path Skill Grounding

Such heterogeneity poses a challenge to scalable skill acquisition, as adversarial knowledge is often manifested at varying levels of fidelity. To bridge this gap, we propose Dual-Path Skill Grounding, a mechanism that maps disparate artifacts into a unified, structured skill space. For methods with existing implementations, we ground skills by reasoning over the source code. Conversely, for methods restricted to natural language, we first reconstruct an executable implementation based on the original documentation and then apply the same extraction procedure to derive skills from the recovered attack logic.

Tri-Axis Skill Validation.

First, functional validity is assessed by applying executable scripts to transform harmful requests in a subset of AdvBench 16, thereby producing adversarial prompts. We then compute the attack success rate of these adversarial prompts against the victim model, e.g., Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct. A skill is considered valid only if its attack success rate exceeds a predefined threshold. Second, schema consistency is evaluated using an LLM-based judge 98, which checks whether adversarial prompts generated by the same skill for different harmful requests preserve a shared schema. Third, behavioral diversity prevents redundancy by computing the embedding similarity between prompts generated by the candidate skill and those produced by existing skills for the same request. A skill is considered diverse only if this similarity is below a predefined threshold.

Example of Extracted Skill.

Each extracted skill consists of an executable script and a corresponding Markdown file. Below, we present an example skill extracted from LogiBreak [54].

A.3 Defense Policy

A.3.1 Analysis of Reward Hacking

Training the defense policy exclusively on adversarial prompts can induce a degenerate refusal-prefix strategy, in which the policy learns to prepend refusals even when the input is benign. This behavior substantially degrades model usability. We demonstrate this failure mode using Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct on GSM8K 17. As shown below, an erroneous refusal prefix causes the model to refuse a harmless mathematical question that it would otherwise answer correctly.

A.3.2 Guard mode of Auxiliary Defense Model

The Guard mode of the learned defense policy essentially functions as a classifier over the generated prefix. To enable rule-based parsing, we deliberately design the SFT data construction pipeline for the defense policy. Specifically, when the defense policy is presented with adversarial prompts, the safe prefixes it generates are constrained to start primarily with phrases such as Please refuse, Warning, or Please refrain. In contrast, for benign prompts, the generated safe prefixes typically begin with Please provide. This design allows our method to introduce almost no additional latency. Alternatively, one could fine-tune a lightweight sentence-transformer model or directly employ an LLM-as-a-judge.

A.4 Efficiency Analysis of Coevolutionary Training

We analyze the computational scaling of EvoSafety under Algorithm 1 and compare it against direct coevolutionary training frameworks between an attacker and a victim, including MAGIC [80] and SSP [73]. Our comparison focuses on the coevolutionary RL stage and excludes initialization costs, such as supervised fine tuning, that may be incurred by individual baselines.

Let KK denote the number of coevolutionary rounds, and let TAT_{A} and TDT_{D} denote the numbers of attack policy and defense policy updates per round, respectively. Let GG be the GRPO group size. Since practical RL training is typically performed with minibatches rather than full dataset sweeps, we denote by BAB_{A} the number of harmful requests used in each attack policy update, by BDadvB_{D}^{\mathrm{adv}} the number of harmful requests used in each defense policy update, and by BDbenB_{D}^{\mathrm{ben}} the number of benign requests used in each defense policy update. Under full batch training, these quantities can instead be set to |𝒟adv||\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{adv}}| and |𝒟ben||\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ben}}|. Let PAP_{A}, PDP_{D}, and PTP_{T} denote the parameter counts of the attacker, the auxiliary defender, and the frozen victim model, respectively. We further distinguish three sequence lengths: LAL_{A} for generated adversarial prompts, LDL_{D} for generated safety prefixes, and LYL_{Y} for victim or defender responses.

Cost model.

Following prior work [34], we use a first order proxy for Transformer generation and policy optimization costs. For a model XX with parameter count PXP_{X} and generated sequence length LL, we define

C^Xgen​(L)=αX​PX​L,C^Xupd​(L)=βX​PX​L,\widehat{C}_{X}^{\mathrm{gen}}(L)=\alpha_{X}P_{X}L,\qquad\widehat{C}_{X}^{\mathrm{upd}}(L)=\beta_{X}P_{X}L, (20)

where C^Xgen\widehat{C}_{X}^{\mathrm{gen}} denotes the proxy autoregressive rollout cost and C^Xupd\widehat{C}_{X}^{\mathrm{upd}} denotes the proxy policy update cost over sampled trajectories. Typically, βX>αX\beta_{X}>\alpha_{X} because policy updates require backward passes, activation storage, and optimizer state operations. The frozen victim model 𝒯\mathcal{T} only incurs generation cost, since its parameters are never updated. This proxy abstracts away implementation dependent constants, prompt prefill costs, hardware utilization, memory bandwidth effects, and details of parallelization. Therefore, we use it only for controlled scaling comparisons under matched rollout budgets, rather than as an exact wall clock estimate. If prompt prefill costs are nonnegligible, the sequence length LL in Eq. 20 can be interpreted as an effective token count that includes both context and generated tokens.

The skill retriever and memory retriever incur additional overheads, denoted by R𝒮R_{\mathcal{S}} and Rℬ​(k)R_{\mathcal{B}}(k), respectively, where Rℬ​(k)R_{\mathcal{B}}(k) may depend on the size of the verified memory bank at round kk. In practice, these retrieval costs are small relative to model rollout and update costs. When reward computation relies on an external judge, the corresponding per trajectory cost can be included as an additional term CjudgeC_{\mathrm{judge}}. We omit this term from the main comparison under the controlled assumption that both frameworks invoke the same judge the same number of times per evaluated trajectory.

Attack phase cost of EvoSafety.

During attack policy optimization, the auxiliary defender and the frozen victim model serve only as evaluators for sampled attacks; only the attacker parameters are updated. For each harmful request, EvoSafety retrieves adversarial skills, samples GG adversarial prompts, retrieves memory support for each prompt, generates the corresponding safety prefix, queries the frozen victim model, and updates the attacker using GRPO group advantages. Omitting judge and memory write costs, the resulting proxy cost is

𝒞^atkours=K​TA​BA​[R𝒮+G⁡(C^Agen​(LA)+C^Aupd​(LA)+Rℬ​(k)+C^Dgen​(LD)+C^Tgen​(LY))].\widehat{\mathcal{C}}_{\mathrm{atk}}^{\mathrm{ours}}=KT_{A}B_{A}\left[R_{\mathcal{S}}+G\left(\widehat{C}_{A}^{\mathrm{gen}}(L_{A})+\widehat{C}_{A}^{\mathrm{upd}}(L_{A})+R_{\mathcal{B}}(k)+\widehat{C}_{D}^{\mathrm{gen}}(L_{D})+\widehat{C}_{T}^{\mathrm{gen}}(L_{Y})\right)\right]. (21)
Defense phase cost of EvoSafety.

During defense policy optimization, the attacker is kept fixed. For each harmful request, the attacker first generates a current adversarial prompt, after which memory support is retrieved. The auxiliary defender then samples GG safety prefixes, and the frozen victim model is queried for each paired safety prefix and attack prompt. For each benign request, EvoSafety retrieves memory support, samples GG safety prefixes, queries the victim model, and computes the reward for the benign branch. Since the attacker and victim model are frozen in this stage, only the auxiliary defender is updated. The resulting proxy cost is

𝒞^defours=KTD[\displaystyle\widehat{\mathcal{C}}_{\mathrm{def}}^{\mathrm{ours}}=KT_{D}\Bigg[ BDadv​(R𝒮+C^Agen​(LA)+Rℬ​(k)+G⁡(C^Dgen​(LD)+C^Dupd​(LD)+C^Tgen​(LY)))\displaystyle B_{D}^{\mathrm{adv}}\Big(R_{\mathcal{S}}+\widehat{C}_{A}^{\mathrm{gen}}(L_{A})+R_{\mathcal{B}}(k)+G\big(\widehat{C}_{D}^{\mathrm{gen}}(L_{D})+\widehat{C}_{D}^{\mathrm{upd}}(L_{D})+\widehat{C}_{T}^{\mathrm{gen}}(L_{Y})\big)\Big) (22)
+BDben(Rℬ(k)+G(C^Dgen(LD)+C^Dupd(LD)+C^Tgen(LY)))].\displaystyle+B_{D}^{\mathrm{ben}}\Big(R_{\mathcal{B}}(k)+G\big(\widehat{C}_{D}^{\mathrm{gen}}(L_{D})+\widehat{C}_{D}^{\mathrm{upd}}(L_{D})+\widehat{C}_{T}^{\mathrm{gen}}(L_{Y})\big)\Big)\Bigg].
Cost of direct coevolutionary frameworks.

In direct coevolutionary training between an attacker and a victim, the defender coincides with the victim model and is responsible for producing the final response. Thus, this setting does not require a separate auxiliary stage for prefix generation followed by a query to a frozen victim model. Under the same adversarial rollout budget, the attack phase has proxy cost

𝒞^atkdirect=K​TA​BA​G​(C^Agen​(LA)+C^Aupd​(LA)+C^Tgen​(LY)).\widehat{\mathcal{C}}_{\mathrm{atk}}^{\mathrm{direct}}=KT_{A}B_{A}G\left(\widehat{C}_{A}^{\mathrm{gen}}(L_{A})+\widehat{C}_{A}^{\mathrm{upd}}(L_{A})+\widehat{C}_{T}^{\mathrm{gen}}(L_{Y})\right). (23)

For defense policy optimization, the direct framework updates the victim or defender model itself. If the direct baseline uses only harmful requests in the defense stage, its proxy cost is

𝒞^defdirect=K​TD​BDadv​[C^Agen​(LA)+G⁡(C^Tgen​(LY)+C^Tupd​(LY))].\widehat{\mathcal{C}}_{\mathrm{def}}^{\mathrm{direct}}=KT_{D}B_{D}^{\mathrm{adv}}\left[\widehat{C}_{A}^{\mathrm{gen}}(L_{A})+G\left(\widehat{C}_{T}^{\mathrm{gen}}(L_{Y})+\widehat{C}_{T}^{\mathrm{upd}}(L_{Y})\right)\right]. (24)

If the direct baseline also includes a benign utility branch, an analogous benign term should be added:

𝒞^defdirect=KTD[\displaystyle\widehat{\mathcal{C}}_{\mathrm{def}}^{\mathrm{direct}}=KT_{D}\Bigg[ BDadv​(C^Agen​(LA)+G⁡(C^Tgen​(LY)+C^Tupd​(LY)))\displaystyle B_{D}^{\mathrm{adv}}\Big(\widehat{C}_{A}^{\mathrm{gen}}(L_{A})+G\big(\widehat{C}_{T}^{\mathrm{gen}}(L_{Y})+\widehat{C}_{T}^{\mathrm{upd}}(L_{Y})\big)\Big) (25)
+BDbenG(C^Tgen(LY)+C^Tupd(LY))].\displaystyle+B_{D}^{\mathrm{ben}}G\big(\widehat{C}_{T}^{\mathrm{gen}}(L_{Y})+\widehat{C}_{T}^{\mathrm{upd}}(L_{Y})\big)\Bigg].
Comparison.

We now compare the two training paradigms under the controlled proxy cost model in Eq. 20. For clarity, we omit the skill and memory retrieval overheads, R𝒮R_{\mathcal{S}} and Rℬ​(k)R_{\mathcal{B}}(k), and assume matched rollout budgets, identical attacker size, and the same use of benign utility evaluation when applicable. Specifically, we assume an 8B attacker model, an 8B victim model 𝒯\mathcal{T}, and a 3B auxiliary defense model 𝒟\mathcal{D} in EvoSafety. Following the approximation in Eq. 20, we take βX=2​αX\beta_{X}=2\alpha_{X} for policy update costs.

Under these assumptions, the attack phase of EvoSafety introduces one additional auxiliary defense generation term relative to direct coevolutionary training:

Δatk=K​TA​BA​G⋅C^Dgen​(LD).\Delta_{\mathrm{atk}}=KT_{A}B_{A}G\cdot\widehat{C}_{D}^{\mathrm{gen}}(L_{D}). (26)

This term corresponds to generating safety prefixes for sampled adversarial prompts.

For the defense phase, the main distinction is that direct coevolutionary training updates the victim or defender model itself, whereas EvoSafety updates only the smaller auxiliary defense model while keeping the victim model frozen. When the direct baseline includes the same benign utility branch as in Eq. 25, the defense stage proxy saving of EvoSafety over direct training is

Sdef=K​TD​(BDadv+BDben)​G​(C^Tupd​(LY)−C^Dgen​(LD)−C^Dupd​(LD)).S_{\mathrm{def}}=KT_{D}(B_{D}^{\mathrm{adv}}+B_{D}^{\mathrm{ben}})G\left(\widehat{C}_{T}^{\mathrm{upd}}(L_{Y})-\widehat{C}_{D}^{\mathrm{gen}}(L_{D})-\widehat{C}_{D}^{\mathrm{upd}}(L_{D})\right). (27)

Thus, EvoSafety is computationally favorable in the coevolutionary RL stage whenever

Sdef>Δatk.S_{\mathrm{def}}>\Delta_{\mathrm{atk}}. (28)

Equivalently, the saving on the defense side from avoiding victim model updates must outweigh the additional cost of auxiliary prefix generation during attack optimization.

Using the linear proxy in Eq. 20, the defense stage saving is positive whenever

βT​PT​LY>(αD+βD)​PD​LD.\beta_{T}P_{T}L_{Y}>(\alpha_{D}+\beta_{D})P_{D}L_{D}. (29)

This condition is expected to hold in the regime targeted by EvoSafety, where the auxiliary defense model is substantially smaller than the victim model and produces shorter safety prefixes, i.e., PD≪PTP_{D}\ll P_{T} and LD<LYL_{D}<L_{Y}. For example, with a 3B auxiliary defender and an 8B victim model, the proxy update cost of the auxiliary defender is substantially smaller than that of updating the victim model; the gap becomes even larger as the victim model scales, e.g., to 70B class models.

Appendix B Experimental Setup

B.1 Attack Skill Library

Specifically, the initial attack skill library is derived from GPTFuzzer 89 and CodeAttack 61. The held-out attack skill library includes methods with released implementations, such as DeepInception 41, ReNeLLM 18, TAP 49, FlipAttack 46, PAP 91, JailbreakingLLMs 13, Logibreak-DEBF 54, QueryAttack 104, Response Attack 50, and StructTransform 88, as well as methods without released code, including Jailbroken 76, SCP 84, and ICL 78. Together, this construction also demonstrates our method’s ability to extract reusable skills from heterogeneous attack papers.

B.2 Adversarial Training Data

To avoid train–test contamination, we rigorously filter the training set to remove not only exact duplicates of HarmBench 48 test samples, but also highly similar instances that may overlap semantically with the evaluation data. Concretely, we encode each sample with Qwen3-Embedding-8B 94 and compute its maximum cosine similarity to the HarmBench 48 set. Samples with similarity above 0.88 are removed. Table 6 reports the resulting sample counts for each dataset.

B.3 Benign Samples in RL-based Defense Training

Benign samples that are intrinsically difficult or exhibit reasoning uncertainty can introduce significant reward noise, where low rewards do not necessarily reflect suboptimal safety prefix generation by the defense model. To mitigate this issue, we curate a high-confidence benign set by leveraging Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct to perform 16 independent reasoning rollouts for each example in GSM8K 17, retaining only those instances that are solved correctly in all runs. We then randomly sample 1,000 such examples to construct the benign dataset for RL-based defense training.

B.4 Datasets for Evaluating General Reasoning Ability

For MMLU 33, we construct the evaluation set by randomly sampling 10 instances from each of the 57 subtasks, resulting in a total of 570 examples. For GSM8K 17, we adopt different evaluation protocols depending on the victim model. Specifically, for Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, we use the full test set. For Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct, we randomly sample 500 examples to improve evaluation efficiency.

B.5 SFT Data Construction for the Attack Model

To equip the attack model with an initial ability to evolve novel adversarial examples from attacks induced by multiple skills, we construct a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) dataset. Specifically, we enumerate pairwise combinations of the skills from GPTFUZZER 61 and use the GPT-4.1 API to synthesize a compositional attack skill for each pair. We then randomly apply these synthesized skills to harmful requests from AdvBench 16, resulting in 20,000 supervised training examples. An illustrative example is shown below, contrasting adversarial prompts derived from individual skills with those induced by the compositional skill.

B.6 SFT Data Construction for the Defense Model

Because the prompt template in the auxiliary defense model explicitly incorporates retrieved adversarial prompts, smaller models (e.g., Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct) tend to over-activate their safety mechanisms. This leads to spurious refusals and impairs their ability to accurately recover the underlying user intent, even for benign queries, as illustrated below.

To mitigate this failure mode, we construct a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) dataset for the defense model that covers both adversarial and benign inputs. The adversarial portion is built from the filtered dataset in Section B.2. For each harmful request, we use Jailbreak-R1 31 to generate 32 attack prompts, which serve as the current user prompts. The benign portion is drawn from the MMLU training set 33, whose examples are used directly as current user prompts. We then use safety prefixes produced by Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct as supervision targets and distill this behavior into a defense model initialized from Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct.

Appendix C Results

C.1 Inference-Time Efficiency

We further analyze the inference efficiency of the proposed defense policy. Specifically, we first collect adversarial prompts from Jailbreak-R1 [31] and then compute the token lengths of the constructed inputs to the defense policy, as shown in Fig. 7 Left. We then measure the inference latency on a H100 GPU. As shown in Fig. 7 Right, benefiting from the lightweight design of our defense policy, which contains only 3B parameters, the latency for each input prompt is generally around 2.5 ms.

C.2 [Skill Validity]: How Effective is the Automated Skill Generation Pipeline?

[Skill Extraction Validity]. We evaluate whether the constructed skills faithfully capture the attack utility of existing jailbreak methods. Specifically, we compare the Attack Success Rate (ASR) of adversarial prompts generated from our constructed skills against those from the original methods. For methods with available executable code, we select CodeAttack [61] and directly generate skills from it. For methods lacking executable code and providing only natural language descriptions, we select Jailbroken 76 and use human-reproduced implementations as a baseline. As shown in Tab. 7, the constructed skills preserve a large fraction of the original effectiveness, despite a consistent performance gap.

[Skill Induction Validity]. We further test whether constructed skills constitute a viable substrate for recursive expansion. Using constructed skills as seeds, we induce new attack variants and compare them against their progenitors. As shown in Tab. 7, induced skills remain competitive and occasionally outperform their seeds at ASR@1, indicating that the skill space supports iterative refinement and exploration without a collapse in attack efficacy. More importantly, achieving a perfect replication of the original methods’ ASR is not the primary objective of our skill library; rather, our goal is to cover a broader spectrum of adversarial prompts. Consequently, the observed marginal decline in ASR under certain settings is acceptable, as the primary contribution lies in providing a scalable and extensible scheme for skill acquisition.

C.3 Impact of Different Defense Methods on General Reasoning Ability

Appendix D Case Studies

D.1 Attack Policy

As illustrated below, we present representative adversarial prompts generated by the trained attack policy. These examples demonstrate that our policy possesses the following capabilities.

(1) When two retrieved skills differ in their attack effectiveness, the policy preferentially exploits prior knowledge about successful attacks. As shown below, the nested prompt from Skill I fails to induce the victim model to generate harmful responses, whereas the nested prompt from Skill II succeeds. Accordingly, our generated adversarial prompts contain almost none of the code-like style from Skill I, while retaining its multi-role narrative structure.

(2) The policy can evolve new attack vectors from existing skills. Beyond adopting the multi-role narrative structure, the policy further constructs two opposing groups of roles, assigns each role responsibility for a subset of the content, and then instructs the victim model to aggregate the partial outputs into a final response. Upon inspection, this divide-and-conquer and adversarial-role strategy does not appear in the training skills, suggesting that the learned attack policy is not merely copying observed templates, but can compose and generalize them into novel attack strategies.

D.2 Defense Policy

D.2.1 Generated Safety Prefix for Benign Queries

Below, we show examples of the safety prefixes generated for benign queries. As can be seen, the generated prefixes are not merely generic prefixes that instruct the model to provide helpful information. Instead, they directly respond to the query itself, namely the calculation related to selling duck eggs.

D.2.2 Generated Safety Prefix for Adversarial Prompts

As illustrated below, when the current input is adversarial, the generated safety prefix does more than instruct the victim model to reject the request. It also explicitly identifies the strategies used by the input to circumvent safety mechanisms, thereby further eliciting the model’s intrinsic defensive capabilities.

D.2.3 Comparison of Defense Policies With and Without Memory Retrieval

We further compare the effect of safe prefixes generated by the defense policy with and without memory retrieval. The defense policy without memory retrieval corresponds to the version re-trained through iterative co-evolutionary training in Tab. 5. As shown, although the prefixes generated by the defense policy without memory retrieval also instruct the model to reject the current input, they cannot compare the current prompt with previously successful attack prompts. Consequently, unlike the prefixes generated by our method, they fail to explicitly identify similarities to prior attacks or report the associated jailbreak strategy, and are therefore less effective at activating the victim model’s endogenous defense mechanisms.

Appendix E Limitations

While our approach demonstrates promising results, we acknowledge several limitations. First, our current evaluation primarily focuses on standalone Large Language Models (LLMs), rather than autonomous agents equipped with tool-use capabilities. Second, the proposed framework does not yet support multimodal inputs. This restricts its applicability in defending vision-enabled models, such as browser-use agents. We leave the extension of our framework to these more complex agentic settings for future work.
